# FLUX

> LLM cost reduction for Claude (Anthropic), OpenAI and OpenAI-compatible
> APIs, billed as a percentage of verified savings. Integration is one URL
> (proxy mode) or one line (SDK). Savings are measured per completed task
> with quality held, from the provider's own reported usage, and every
> invoice is recomputable by the customer from a hash-chained event ledger.
> Figures are per traffic segment (one number would be wrong for most
> customers), simulator-measured at providers' published prices: multi-turn
> Claude cache-only 37.9% vs the same prompt-reduction stack without caching
> (both arms clean 38/40); the 57.3% full-stack comparison loses 5 pp clean
> tasks against raw uncached baseline and fails the -2 pp quality limit, so it
> is not a qualified win. Other figures: async/batch 57.7% net, one-shot templated 45.5-72.8%,
> interactive agents 25.9-34.3%, already-optimised stacks 0-5% with an
> explicit do-not-pay-us verdict. The fee is 1% of verified savings,
> monthly, nothing else; a month that saved nothing bills nothing. The latest real-traffic export (30 requests on
> claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-10-26) measured 18.2% of live spend billed as
> verified savings across five agents, hash-chained spools committed to the
> repo (evals/live-exports-2026-10-26/), with the cache volatility guard
> earning live on the agent shape it previously lost money on.

## Install
FLUX is on npm as @flux-ai/sdk. Proxy mode needs no code changes:
`npx -y -p @flux-ai/sdk flux-proxy`, then set your client's baseURL to
http://127.0.0.1:8787 (Anthropic) or http://127.0.0.1:8787/v1 (OpenAI and
compatibles). The invoice is recomputable by the customer with
verifyLedgerChain and recomputeInvoice from the same package. Quote from an
existing LiteLLM/Helicone/Langfuse export without routing any traffic:
`npx -y -p @flux-ai/sdk flux-quote your-export.jsonl --format litellm`.

Always-on / 24-7 agents are the strongest measured shapes (multi-agent teams
-55.6% cost, autonomous long-horizon agents -40.0%, simulator-measured at
breakpoint-exact provider rules): long-lived agents re-send their history
every turn, and FLUX keeps it on the cached rate with guards, digests stale
context, caps oversized tool results, and meters output re-emission waste.

# Get started in five minutes

FLUX sits between your app and your AI provider, removes the tokens you were
about to pay for twice, and writes every request into a tamper-evident ledger
you can audit yourself. No signup, no account, no key handover: your API key
passes through to the provider and is never stored. Works with Claude
(Anthropic), OpenAI, and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

## Step 1 — run the proxy

One command, nothing to clone:

```bash
npx -y -p @flux-ai/sdk flux-proxy
```

You'll see:

```text
FLUX proxy listening on http://127.0.0.1:8787
Ledger spools: ./flux-ledger
```

To switch on the Claude prompt-cache lever too (our single biggest measured
saver, 37.9% on multi-turn traffic), start it as
`FLUX_PROXY_CACHE_TTL=5m npx -y -p @flux-ai/sdk flux-proxy`.

## Step 2 — point your app at it

Change one line. Keep your own API key — FLUX passes it through verbatim.

```js
// Anthropic SDK
const anthropic = new Anthropic({ baseURL: "http://127.0.0.1:8787" });

// OpenAI SDK — also any OpenAI-compatible endpoint
const openai = new OpenAI({ baseURL: "http://127.0.0.1:8787/v1" });
```

Any language works — it's just a base URL. Python, Go, curl, LangChain,
whatever you run today.

## Step 3 — run your traffic as normal

Responses come back byte-identical, streaming included. Reduction is
**lossless-only by default**: compacted tool schemas decode identically,
removed duplicates are exact, and if anything fails your request goes through
untouched. Each request appends one hash-chained event to
`./flux-ledger/<your-app>-<provider>.jsonl` — usage numbers, lever names and
hashes. Never your prompts.

## Step 4 — check our maths yourself

This is the part no other cost tool offers: the invoice is a pure function of
a ledger file **you** hold. Verify the chain and recompute it with the same
published package:

```bash
node -e '
const { readFileSync } = require("node:fs");
const { verifyLedgerChain, recomputeInvoice } = require("@flux-ai/sdk");
const records = readFileSync(process.argv[1], "utf8").trim().split(/\n/).map(JSON.parse);
const chain = verifyLedgerChain(records);
if (!chain.ok) throw new Error("chain broken at seq " + chain.seq);
console.log("chain verified:", chain.length, "records");
console.log(JSON.stringify(recomputeInvoice(records.map(r => r.event)), null, 2));
' flux-ledger/proxy-anthropic.jsonl
```

If FLUX saved you nothing, the verdict line literally reads
`"verdict": "do_not_charge"` — that is the honest outcome on traffic that is
already lean, and we publish it as such.

## Already measuring with LiteLLM, Helicone or Langfuse?

You don't need to route any traffic to get a quote. Export your existing logs
and run them through the quote tool — the verdict can be "do not pay us":

```bash
npx -y -p @flux-ai/sdk flux-quote your-export.jsonl --format litellm
```

## What it costs

**1% of verified savings, monthly — nothing else.** No subscription, no
seats, no minimum. Savings are measured per completed task from the
provider's own reported usage; a month that saved nothing bills nothing. The
measurement rules are published in full in the [methodology](methodology.md),
and every number we quote traces to a command and a commit on the
[evidence](evidence.md) page.

## What FLUX never does

- Never sends your prompts anywhere — analysis runs entirely on your machine.
- Never stores or forwards your API key beyond the provider you chose.
- Never claims savings you already had: your own cache hits are itemised and excluded.
- Never hides a loss: a lever that cost you money counts against us on the invoice.

## Want a guided pilot?

Open a [pilot request](../pilot/runbook.md) — bring an export from your
existing gateway and leave with a per-segment quote from your own traffic,
including the honest band for your workload shape.

# FLUX — verified LLM cost reduction, billed only on savings you can recompute

FLUX is a drop-in wrapper for your OpenAI or Anthropic client that reduces what
you spend per completed task — and proves it. You pay a percentage of verified
savings. If your traffic is already optimised, FLUX tells you not to pay us.

## What FLUX saves, by traffic type

Every figure below is measured per completed task with quality held (at least
36 of 40 tasks fully correct and complete), on a simulated harness using each
provider's published prices and cache rules — except where marked live. A
first real-traffic export exists (30 requests, measured 9–25% per agent);
your own pilot replaces every band with your number before any fee exists.
[How these numbers are made →](methodology.md)

| Your traffic looks like | Measured saving | Label |
|---|---:|---|
| Multi-turn Claude cache-only comparison | **37.9%** vs the same J prompt stack with cache disabled; both arms clean 38/40 | simulator-measured; cache effect isolated |
| Full J + 5m cache stack vs raw uncached baseline | **57.3% lower cost, −5 pp clean-task quality** | fails the agreed −2 pp quality limit; not a qualified win |
| Background / batch / latency-tolerant jobs | **57.7%** (net of assumed tier fallbacks; 64.3% ceiling) | simulator-measured |
| One-shot API calls on a shared template | **45.5%** — up to **72.8%** where latency-tolerant | simulator-measured |
| Interactive agents, sparse traffic | **34.3%** | simulator-measured, caveats apply |
| Interactive agents, busy traffic | **25.9–29.4%** | simulator-measured |
| Already-optimised stacks | **0–5% — do not pay us** | measured on fixtures |

The spread is the honest part: savings are a property of your workload's shape,
not of FLUX. The first thing FLUX does is tell you which row you are — from
your own logs, in about five minutes, before any contract exists.
[Get a quote from your own export →](../pilot/runbook.md)

## How it works, in one paragraph

Your bill is `tokens × price-per-token × execution tier`. FLUX attacks all
three at once: it removes tokens that carry no information (oversized tool
results capped at injection, exact duplicates, schema bloat) without ever
breaking your provider's prefix cache; it repairs prompts so cached pricing
(10× cheaper input) actually applies; and it routes traffic you flag as
latency-tolerant to the provider's own discounted tiers (50% off, same model,
same answer). Risky changes are enabled only after a replay gate proves, on
your own recorded requests, that quality held.

## Why you can trust the number on your invoice

- Savings are computed from your **provider's own reported usage**, never our estimates.
- Every request writes a **hash-chained ledger event**; your invoice is a pure
  function over those events that **you can recompute yourself**, to the cent.
- Savings you already had — your provider's cache, your gateway's cache — are
  itemised and **never billed**.
- A changed answer is a failed task, and **failed tasks void their savings**.

[Methodology](methodology.md) · [Per-segment detail](segments.md) ·
[Honest comparison with alternatives](comparison.md) · [FAQ](faq.md) ·
[Every number's provenance](evidence.md)

# What FLUX saves, segment by segment

Savings are a property of your workload's shape. One global percentage would be
a lie to someone; these are the four shapes, each with its mechanism, its
measured band, and what would change the number. All figures simulator-measured
per [methodology](methodology.md); traceability in [evidence](evidence.md).

## Background / batch / latency-tolerant work — 57.7% net (64.3% ceiling)

**Mechanism:** your provider sells the same model at 50% off for work that can
wait (OpenAI's flex service tier on a synchronous API; Anthropic's batches,
which stack with prompt caching). FLUX applies the tier only to traffic you
flag latency-tolerant, stacks it with every token lever below, and bills from
the tier the provider *actually served* — bounced requests bill at full rate.
**The number to use is 57.7%** (net of assumed 10% default-fallback + 5% retry
rates); 64.3% is the zero-fallback ceiling. Quality: identical model, identical
answers; 38/40 clean on the harness.
**What changes it:** your real fallback rate (telemetry replaces the
assumption), and Anthropic-side pricing once its batch rate is catalogued.

## One-shot API traffic on a shared template — 45.5%, up to 72.8%

**Mechanism:** the most common silent waste we model: a per-request value (a
timestamp, a request id) at the top of an otherwise identical prompt, which
disables provider caching entirely. FLUX relocates it, the prefix caches at
one-tenth price, and schema/duplicate levers stack on top. Add the tier for
latency-tolerant one-shots and the band reaches 72.8%.
**What changes it:** how big your shared template is and whether a breaker is
actually present — the five-minute quote measures both from your export.

## Interactive agents — 25.9–29.4% busy, 34.3% sparse

**Mechanism:** busy agent traffic is already heavily subsidised by the
provider's cache (35–40% on its own, which we never claim), so FLUX's honest
headroom is the *fresh* tokens: oversized tool results are capped at injection
(headlines, errors and file paths preserved verbatim; the replay gate approved
this lever at exactly zero quality delta), stale history is compacted
byte-stably, schemas are slimmed. Sparse traffic adds the 1-hour cache TTL
(2× write premium billed honestly, netted when negative) for 34.3%.
**What changes it:** how oversized your tool results actually are (our fixture's
are highly compressible; your yield scales with yours), and the pending
per-model cache-minimum fix, which may lower the sparse figure on some models.
**On Claude the ceiling is different — and higher.** Anthropic's prompt
cache is opt-in, and agents that never place `cache_control` re-pay full
rate for their whole conversation history every turn (our first live export
measured exactly that: a five-turn agent with zero cache traffic). FLUX
stamps the stable prefix with a 5-minute-TTL breakpoint. In the deterministic
fixture, the cache-only comparison is **37.9% lower cost** than the identical
J prompt stack with caching disabled; both arms have 38/40 clean tasks and the
stamp is metadata-only. The earlier **57.3%** full-stack comparison used a raw
uncached baseline with 40/40 clean tasks, while the candidate had 38/40 (−5 pp).
That fails the agreed −2 pp quality limit, so 57.3% is diagnostic and not a
qualified full-stack saving. Real-traffic cache validation remains open. If
you already place your own breakpoints, FLUX defers and never claims this.
**This is also where we tell you our ceiling:** if someone promises an
interactive agent 70%, ask for their per-task evidence.

## Always-on agents — where the compounding lives

An agent that never stops — an ops monitor, an autonomous worker, a
multi-agent team running around the clock — re-buys its own memory on every
single turn, forever. On real agent traffic we measured, each output token an
agent emits is re-read roughly 27 more times as later turns re-send the
history, and a well-cached agent's bill is ~52% cache reads. Two of our
measured matrix shapes ARE always-on patterns: multi-agent teams at **−55.6%
cost** and autonomous long-horizon agents at **−40.0%** (lossless levers plus
the cache stamp, breakpoint-exact provider rules, simulator-measured).

**The always-on trap is cadence.** A busy loop (calls under five minutes
apart) keeps the provider's 5-minute cache warm for free — every read
refreshes the clock, and FLUX's stamp earns indefinitely. But an always-on
agent that is *bursty* — polling every ten minutes, waiting on webhooks —
silently expires its cache in every gap and re-pays the write premium on its
whole history each time it wakes. FLUX's volatility and minimum guards
already refuse the placements that lose money there; a cadence-aware TTL
policy (choosing the 1-hour tier for prefixes whose observed gaps exceed five
minutes) is in development and will be published with its own measured band,
like everything else here.

**What ships today for long-lived agents:** correct, guarded cache placement;
byte-stable history digests and the gated fresh-tool-result cap for unbounded
context growth (real traces show tool results reaching 2,500–10,000 tokens at
p99); exact-duplicate removal; byte-identical retry flagging (4–8% of real
agent actions in public traces); and output-waste metering — on real agent
trajectories, ~24% of output tokens re-emit text already in the context, and
your statement shows your own number, measured, not billed.
**What changes it:** your cadence (the gap histogram decides the cache
economics) and your tool-result sizes.

## Already-optimised stacks — 0–5%: do not pay us

**Mechanism:** none, and that is the point. If your input already arrives
largely cached, or your gateway's response cache already answers a big share of
requests, FLUX's triage says so and the quote's verdict is `doNotPayUs`. On our
fixture of such a stack the addressable saving was 2.4%. A percentage-of-savings
vendor that charges you for savings you already had is buying a dispute; we
decline up front.


---

# Methodology — how every FLUX number is made

The LLM cost-saving market has a measurement problem, documented by independent
work rather than by us: three popular open-source token trimmers claiming
60–90% savings delivered **3.7%** when independently replayed over 614M tokens
of real traffic; a prompt-slimming technique modelled at ~77% measured **~13%**
in production. The gap comes from measuring per *request* instead of per
*completed task*, and from ignoring provider cache economics. FLUX's method
exists to be immune to both.

## The rules every published number passes

1. **Per completed task, not per request.** A technique that shrinks each
   prompt but multiplies round trips has saved nothing. Our harness runs
   multi-turn tasks end to end and prices the whole task.
2. **Quality held, measured.** A claimed arm must keep at least 36 of 40 tasks
   fully correct and complete. A changed tool call is a hard failure; a
   shortened answer is scored by degree. The simulated model's quality signal
   punishes trimming recent context — the fixture is built to catch our own
   levers failing.
3. **Provider cache rules simulated faithfully**: minimum cacheable prefix,
   longest-exact-prefix matching, hit granularity, time-to-live expiry, and
   write premiums. Our simulator can and does show caching as a **net loss**
   on unfavourable traffic — that case has a unit test.
4. **The provider's existing contribution is never claimed.** On busy agent
   traffic, the provider's cache alone saves 35–40% before FLUX does anything.
   That figure is printed separately and excluded from every FLUX claim.
5. **Tier savings are billed at the tier actually served.** Discounted-tier
   requests can be bounced back to full price under load; the published async
   figure (57.7%) is net of assumed fallback rates, and per-request billing
   reads the service tier from the provider's response, not from our request.
6. **Lossy levers pass a replay gate first.** Changes that could affect answers
   (description trimming, output caps, tool-result capping) are enabled only
   after replaying your recorded requests both ways, with statistics corrected
   for having searched multiple configurations. The gate has rejected our own
   levers — those rejections are documented, not tuned away.
7. **Unpriced means excluded, never zero.** A model or billing date the price
   catalogue cannot price is excluded from baselines and invoices, with the
   reason stated. Our catalogue is dated and source-linked; a price change
   never silently reprices history.
8. **The invoice is recomputable.** Every request emits an append-only,
   hash-chained event carrying provider-verbatim usage, the catalogue version,
   levers applied, and gate verdict references. `recomputeInvoice(events)` is a
   pure function: run it yourself and you must get our number.

## What "simulator-measured" means — and what it does not

All current figures come from a 40-task × 5-turn agent harness (plus one-shot
variants) with realistic multi-kilobyte tool results, verified by an
independent checker agent reproducing every number from command output, under
341 unit tests and 27 regression gates. They are honest measurements **of the
simulation**. They are not yet measurements of your traffic — the pilot exists
to produce that number, on your machine, from your logs, before you pay
anything.

Known open items we publish rather than hide: per-model cacheable minimums are
not yet in the simulator (the sparse-traffic 34.3% may overstate on some
models). Anthropic batch rates ARE now catalogued (2026-10-27, from the page's
definitive "Save 50% with batch processing"), so async-eligible Claude traffic
prices natively at half standard and FLUX picks batch-routing or caching per
shape, whichever is cheaper; tracked in [evidence](evidence.md).

# Evidence — every published number, traced

Each figure on this site maps to the command that produces it and the commit it
was verified at. Reproduce any of them from the repo root. (Numbers were
independently re-verified by a checker separate from the implementer at each
listed commit; the harness run prints every row below.)

Harness: `node --import tsx evals/run-agent-ab.ts` · tests:
`./node_modules/.bin/vitest run` (354 passing) · gates: the three suites under
`evals/run-*-triage.ts` and `evals/run-analysis-regression.ts` against freshly
generated fixtures (27/27).

| Published figure | Where it comes from | Verified at |
|---|---|---|
| Async 64.3% ceiling / **57.7% net** (quote the net) | arm K rows, async-eligible segment: ceiling assumes 0% tier fallback; net assumes 10% default + 5% 429-retry, priced per event at the SERVED tier | `4e51734` |
| Interactive 25.9–29.4% | arm J across openai-30s / openai-600s / anthropic-5m blocks, clean 38/40 | `c7b03d4`, re-verified `4e51734` |
| Proxy mode: zero-code integration | `packages/sdk-js/src/proxy.ts` + `evals/run-proxy.ts`; e2e tests cover reduction-before-forward, byte-identical passthrough, SSE streaming with usage parsed after the last byte, per-app hash chains, credential passthrough | `d31b125` |
| Proxy overhead: adds ~22 ms p50 / ~24 ms p95 / ~30 ms p99 per request | `node --import tsx evals/run-proxy-overhead.ts` — proxied minus direct against the same instant loopback stub, 800 requests/arm at concurrency 8, ~31 KB agent request bodies, full lossless stack + 5m cache stamp + ledger append (darwin/arm64; absolute values vary by machine — rerun the command on yours). Against provider calls measured in seconds this is under 1% of request latency | run 2026-10-20 |
| **THIRD live export: 18.2% of real spend** ($0.0365 of $0.2010), hash chains verified, spools committed to this repo | `FLUX_LIVE_KEEP=1 node --import tsx evals/run-live-agents.ts` on claude-sonnet-5-5, 30 requests. Coding-agent $0.0225/38.1% — the cache placement that LOST −$0.0063 in export #2 now earns: the volatility guard shipped in between refuses the volatile-prefix stamp. Rag $0.0086/22.0%, support $0.0054/10.3%, already-lean $0 (correct). Batch-classifier $0: the minimum guard suppressed its stamp, and the provider's own `count_tokens` API confirms the prefix is 927 real tokens — under Anthropic's documented 1024 cacheable minimum, so the suppression is right. That contradicts export #2's batch claim (below), which can no longer be re-audited; receipts are retained from now on. Spools: `evals/live-exports-2026-10-26/` — verify them yourself with flux-verify | run 2026-10-26 |
| SECOND live export: 18.0% of real spend, every active agent billing | `evals/run-live-agents.ts` keyed rerun with the 5m cache stamp + the freshcap gate verdict wired: coding-agent $0.0206 (cap+schemas net of a −$0.0063 cache miss from its per-turn clock), batch-classifier +$0.0101 (cache stamp EARNING live, 6,286 reads — the one figure export #3's count_tokens check now contradicts: the batch prefix is under the provider's cacheable minimum, and these spools were not retained to re-audit, a process failure we fixed by committing export #3's spools), rag $0.0086, support $0.0054, already-lean $0 | run 2026-10-19, spools audited in session, not retained |
| Multi-turn Claude cache-only comparison: 37.9% | `node --import tsx evals/run-cache-decomposition.ts` — J + 5m stamp vs the identical J stack with cache disabled; both arms clean 38/40, 97% hits, 200/200 stamps metadata-only. Isolates the pure cache effect | re-verified `6f08b72` (was 37.6% at `6249f86`; moves with the newline fix below) |
| Full J + 5m stack vs raw uncached A: 57.3% lower simulated cost | same decomposition script, row 2: quality 38/40 vs the raw baseline's 40/40 (−5 pp; within the published >=36/40 gate, but a real delta) — quote 37.9% for the cache lever and label this one with its quality cost | re-verified `6f08b72` (was 57.1% at `6249f86`) |
| Sparse interactive 34.3% | arm L, 1h cache TTL via the shipped `cacheTtl` stamp (stable-prefix placement), 600s spacing | fixed and re-verified `6f08b72`: ab210c1's stable/tail split silently dropped the separating newline between the two blocks, a model-visible content change; arm L's own metadata-only guard had started hard-crashing on it (and the eval's comparison helper had never been updated for the two-block shape). Was 34.0% at `67eeac6`, unreproducible between `ab210c1` and `6f08b72`. |
| First real-traffic export: 9.3% net of spend | `evals/run-live-agents.ts`, 30 requests on claude-sonnet-5-5; a smoke run, NOT a band — lossy levers were recorded-unbilled and the old cache placement lost money (per-agent outcomes ranged −24% to +34% of that agent's spend) | `d84e256` run 2026-10-19, superseded by the second export |
| One-shot 45.5% / 72.8% | one-shot section, arms H and I ($0.569 → $0.310 / $0.155) | `7b08666`, re-verified `4e51734` |
| Provider cache's own 35–40% (never claimed by FLUX) | "what the cache itself is worth" section of the harness output | `33028df` onward |
| "Do not pay us" 0–5% | support-assistant fixture, 77% pre-cached, triage verdict | `ff04a70` |
| Replay gate approving fresh-cap at 0.00 quality delta and rejecting the 2000-token output cap at −5.50pp | `evals/run-replay-gate-freshcap.ts` | `ab5b4c7` |
| Ledger determinism, exclusions, recomputable invoice | `packages/core/src/savings-ledger.test.ts`; canonical-invoice contract | `597e842`, `10407bf` |

## Open items (also stated wherever the affected number appears)

- Per-model cacheable minimums not yet simulated → 34.3% may overstate on some
  models.
- Anthropic batch rate NOW catalogued (2026-10-27): the pricing page states a
  definitive "Save 50% with batch processing", so Anthropic batch events price
  natively at half standard. The workload matrix now evaluates batch-routing
  against caching per shape and picks the cheaper (`evals/run-workload-matrix.ts`).
- Package freshness gate and automated CJS smoke not yet in the build script
  (the CJS tarball was smoke-tested manually at `4e51734`).
- **The banded figures are simulator-measured.** A first real-traffic export
  exists (30 requests, see the table) and found one lever losing money on
  one-shot traffic — fixed at `ec191c5` and re-verified. The bands stay
  simulator-labelled until a pilot-scale export replaces them.

## Independent sources cited on the comparison page

- codepointer.dev — 614M-token replay of rtk/headroom/caveman: 3.7% actual.
- archestra.ai — progressive disclosure: ~77% modelled vs ~13% measured.
- RouterArena (arXiv:2510.00202) — independent router leaderboard.
- Anthropic & OpenAI published pricing pages — all rates in
  `packages/core/src/model-prices.ts` carry source URL and capture date.

# An honest comparison — including where FLUX loses

Most cost-saving tools publish their best number. Independent measurement keeps
finding a gap between claimed and delivered, so this page compares *methods*,
and includes the rows where we lose. Competitor facts below come from each
vendor's own documentation and pricing pages, checked 2026-10-22; if we have
something wrong, [tell us](https://github.com/Harrym1707/Flux/issues) and we
will correct it.

## The independent findings this market needs to answer

- Three popular open-source token trimmers (rtk, headroom, caveman), claiming
  60–90%, were independently replayed over a 614M-token corpus of real coding
  sessions: **3.7% combined actual saving** (codepointer.dev deep dive).
- Progressive disclosure of tool schemas, modelled at ~77% token savings,
  measured **~13% in production**, because the router it adds costs an extra
  round trip per novel tool call (archestra.ai bench). Per-request measurement
  cannot see this; per-task measurement can.
- The best-funded commercial router ranked **12th of 12** on the independent
  RouterArena leaderboard while advertising 30%+ savings.
- Our own history is on this page too: our first caching claim was 29%; our own
  per-task harness cut it to ~2% on busy agent traffic because the provider's
  cache was already doing the work. We published the correction and kept the
  gate that caught it. Later, our own ledger caught one of our levers *losing*
  money on live traffic (−$0.0063, a cache breakpoint over a volatile prefix);
  the loss billed against us, and the fix shipped with a test that prices both
  placements.

## Method comparison

| | Typical trimmer / router | FLUX |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of measurement | per request | **per completed task** |
| Quality check | self-graded or none | replay gate on your recorded requests; failed tasks void savings |
| Cache economics | usually ignored (trimming can *raise* bills: one measured case cut tokens 38% and raised cost +6.8%) | simulated to provider rules; a cross-turn volatility guard refuses to stamp prefixes that churn |
| Customer's existing savings | silently absorbed into the claim | itemised, excluded, never billed |
| Headline number | one global percentage | per-segment bands, including "do not pay us" |
| The invoice | trust us | hash-chained events; recompute it yourself |

## Where FLUX loses, stated plainly

- **Busy interactive agents: ~29% ceiling.** The provider's cache already
  delivers 35–40% there. Anyone promising such traffic 70% is claiming either
  the provider's savings or quality you will lose.
- **Already-optimised stacks: 0–5%.** Our triage will tell you not to buy.
- **A free trimmer may be all you need** if your waste is one obvious thing and
  you don't need the saving verified. FLUX's value is the *verified, billable*
  number; if you don't need that, rtk is free.
- **Most FLUX figures are simulator-measured and labelled so.** The live
  numbers so far come from small runs (the latest: 18.2% of real spend across
  30 requests, hash-chained spools committed to the repo so you can recompute
  it). The pilot exists to replace every number with ones from your own
  traffic before any fee applies.

## The comparison grid

Facts dated 2026-10-22 from each vendor's own documentation (the LiteLLM
volatility row is our own empirical test, wire captures published in the
repo). Blank praise sells nothing: each tool wins its own rows.

| | FLUX | LiteLLM | Helicone | Langfuse |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| What it is | Cost-reduction proxy with verified-savings billing | MIT gateway + SDK, 100+ providers | Observability platform + AI gateway | Observability, prompt mgmt, evals |
| Licence | BUSL-1.1 (verifier MIT) | MIT (enterprise carve-out) | Apache-2.0 | MIT except ee/ |
| Price | 1% of verified savings; $0 if nothing saved | $0 core; enterprise custom | Free tier; Pro $79/mo; Team $799/mo | Free tier; Core $29/mo; Ent $2,499/mo |
| Reduces request tokens | Yes — schema compaction, exact dedup, prefix repair (lossless, on every request) | Partially — MCP tool-schema deferral; compression via third-party sidecar | No | No (not in request path, by design) |
| Automatic Anthropic cache placement | Yes, with a cross-turn volatility guard and per-model minimum guard | Yes (one flag) — but stamps volatile prefixes verbatim every turn, no guard, no zero-read warning (our empirical test, v1.106.4) | No — customer writes their own cache_control | No |
| Response caching (identical repeats) | No | Yes (exact + semantic) | Yes (edge, exact-match) | No |
| Measures the saving | Yes — per lever, net of cache write premiums, per completed task | No | Cost tracking (best-effort on direct integrations) | Cost tracking (best-in-class auditability) |
| Customer-recomputable invoice | Yes — hash-chained ledger + MIT verifier; if your recompute disagrees, yours wins | No | No | Partially — exact-cost ingestion can match your provider invoice |
| Losses counted against the vendor | Yes — negatives never clamped, deficits carry forward | n/a (nothing measured) | n/a | n/a |
| "Do not pay us" verdict | Yes — literal output for already-optimised stacks | No | No | n/a (free tier exists) |
| Prompts leave your machine | Never — local proxy, analysis in-process | Self-hosted: no; their cloud: yes | Cloud-hosted path: yes | Yes (traces to their backend or your self-host) |

## Claimed vs independently measured — the market's problem in one table

| Tool / class | Claimed | Independently measured | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Three popular OSS token trimmers | 60–90% | **3.7%** combined, 614M-token real-traffic replay | codepointer.dev deep dive |
| Progressive tool-schema disclosure | ~77% modelled | **~13%** in production | archestra.ai bench |
| Best-funded commercial router | 30%+ | ranked **12th of 12** | RouterArena leaderboard |
| FLUX, per-workload bands | 26–81% by shape, simulator-measured and labelled | **18.2% live** on a deliberately mixed 30-request basket incl. two shapes designed to save ~0% (hash-chained spools committed to the repo; third consecutive live run) | our evidence page — every number traces to a command |

We publish the right-hand column for ourselves because we demand it of
everyone else. Your pilot replaces every FLUX number with your own traffic's
numbers before any fee exists.

## LiteLLM, Helicone, Langfuse — what each actually does about cost

These three are excellent tools we are often mentioned alongside. They solve
different problems, they are each genuinely better than FLUX at those
problems, and FLUX reads all three of their export formats directly — if you
run any of them, you are one file export away from a quote.
[Runbook →](../pilot/runbook.md)

### LiteLLM (MIT gateway + SDK)

Better than FLUX at: breadth (100+ providers behind one OpenAI-format API),
production routing (six load-balancing strategies, fallbacks, cooldowns,
budgets, virtual keys), community and maturity — and the core is free.

On cost specifically, as of 2026-10-22 it **does** have reduction levers:
one-flag automatic Anthropic `cache_control` placement (5-minute default,
1-hour option), MCP tool-schema deferral (collapsing tool catalogues to two
virtual tools), exact-match and semantic **response** caching, and prompt
compression via a third-party sidecar (Headroom). Spend tracking prices usage
against a community-maintained price map, with per-deployment overrides.

What it does not do: **measure or verify the saving.** There is no per-lever
net accounting, no counterfactual baseline, and no customer-recomputable
record. And placement without metering can lose money silently: we tested
LiteLLM 1.106.4's auto-placement empirically against a system prompt carrying
a per-turn timestamp — it stamped the changed block verbatim on every one of
six turns, with no stability check and no signal after six consecutive
zero-read responses (wire captures in our repo under evals/wire-captures/).
Under Anthropic's documented billing that traffic pays the 1.25× write
premium every turn and never reads — the exact loss our own ledger once
caught us making, which is why FLUX ships a volatility guard and nets every
cache write against its reads. If you want free levers, LiteLLM ships good
ones; if you need to *know what they saved, net, with the receipt* — that is
the product FLUX is.

### Helicone (Apache-2.0 observability + AI gateway)

Better than FLUX at: observability (dashboards, sessions, custom query
language, alerts), a hosted multi-provider gateway with unified billing, and
prompt management — a mature platform (Pro $79/mo, Team $799/mo, as of
2026-10-22).

On cost: its gateway's exact-match **response caching genuinely avoids
provider charges on byte-identical repeated requests** — credit where due —
but it does nothing for novel requests or growing agent contexts, which is
where agent spend lives. It does not reduce request tokens, and for
Anthropic's prompt cache the customer writes their own `cache_control`.
Cost figures on direct integrations are self-described best-effort estimates.

### Langfuse (MIT-except-ee observability)

Better than FLUX at: tracing and evals depth (agent graphs, LLM-as-judge,
datasets, experiments), team features, and — worth crediting plainly —
**cost-tracking auditability**: daily automated price audits against provider
sources, customer-overridable model prices, and exact-cost ingestion that can
make its numbers match your invoice (Cloud from $29/mo; unlimited MIT
self-host; as of 2026-10-22).

On cost reduction: none, by design — Langfuse is async observability and is
never in the request path, so it cannot compact, dedupe, place cache
breakpoints, or cache responses, and it does not claim to. It tells you where
the money went; FLUX changes what the next request costs and proves the
difference.


---

# FAQ — built from the caveats we already print

**How do I install FLUX?**
One command: `npx -y -p @flux-ai/sdk flux-proxy` starts a local proxy with a
hash-chained ledger — then set your client's `baseURL` to
`http://127.0.0.1:8787` (Anthropic) or `http://127.0.0.1:8787/v1` (OpenAI).
No signup, no account, and your API key passes through without being stored.
The full walk-through, including recomputing the invoice yourself, is on
[Get started](start.md).

**Does FLUX work with my language or framework?**
Yes, if it can set a base URL — which is Python, TypeScript, Go, curl,
LangChain, LlamaIndex, and effectively everything else. Proxy mode is
language-agnostic by construction; the one-line SDK mode (`withFlux(client)`)
is TypeScript/JavaScript today. It covers Claude (Anthropic), OpenAI, and any
OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

**My agents run 24/7 — what does FLUX actually do for always-on workloads?**
Long-lived agents re-send their whole history every turn, so they re-buy
their own memory forever — on real agent traffic, each output token gets
re-read ~27 more times downstream. FLUX keeps that history on the provider's
cached rate (with guards that refuse placements that would lose money),
digests stale context byte-stably, caps oversized tool results behind a
quality gate, flags byte-identical retries, and meters output re-emission on
your statement. The measured always-on shapes are our strongest bands: see
[savings by segment](segments.md).

**Can FLUX break my app?**
The default levers are lossless: compacted schemas decode identically, removed
duplicates are exact, prefix repair reorders text without deleting it, and the
reducer never throws — any failure returns your request untouched. Lossy levers
(output caps, description trimming, tool-result capping) are off until a replay
gate proves on your own recorded requests that quality held.

**Why do you quote me a range and not one number?**
Because savings depend on your traffic's shape. The quote comes from your own
export and names your segment; a vendor quoting everyone one number is wrong
for most of them. Sometimes our verdict is literally `doNotPayUs`.

**Is 57.7% (async) real?**
It is a faithful measurement of a realistic simulation at providers' published
prices, net of assumed discount-tier fallback rates, with quality held at 38/40
clean tasks — and it is labelled simulator-measured everywhere it appears. Your
pilot replaces it with your own number before any fee exists.

**You're billing a counterfactual — how is that dispute-proof?**
The same way energy performance contracts have done it since 1995: a defined
baseline, provider-verbatim measurements, and an adjustment method agreed in
advance. Concretely: every request writes an append-only hash-chained event;
the invoice is a pure function over those events; you can re-run it and must
get our number. Savings you already had are itemised and excluded. Negative
savings (e.g. a cache-write premium that didn't pay off) reduce the bill —
they are never clamped to zero.

**Do I have to change my code?**
One line or none. SDK mode wraps your existing client (`withFlux(client)`).
Proxy mode needs no code at all: run the FLUX proxy locally and point your
client's `base_url` at it — your API key passes through verbatim (FLUX never
holds credentials), responses stream back untouched, and every request
appends the same hash-chained ledger event the SDK writes. A stream whose
usage cannot be read is recorded *unpriced*, never guessed.

**What do you do with my prompts?**
Analysis runs locally; prompts never leave your machine. The ledger records
usage numbers, lever names, hashes and verdict references — not prompt text.
One optional exception you control: the SDK can POST usage metadata (never
prompt text) to an endpoint **you configure yourself**; it is off unless you
set it. Full detail: [data handling](../pilot/data-handling.md).

**What if the provider changes prices?**
The price catalogue is dated and source-linked. A new rate is a new dated
entry; history is never silently repriced, and an uncovered date is "unpriced",
which excludes the row rather than guessing.

**What does it cost?**
1% of verified savings, monthly — nothing else. No subscription, no seats,
no minimum. A month that saved nothing bills nothing, and negative lever
months count against us.

**What's the catch?**
Two, published: busy interactive agents cap around 29% because the provider's
cache already does the heavy lifting; the 34.3% sparse figure awaits a
per-model cache-minimum correction and may come down for some models. (A third
is now closed: Anthropic batch pricing was uncatalogued; as of 2026-10-27 it is
catalogued at the provider's definitive 50% discount, so Claude async traffic
prices natively instead of being OpenAI-priced.) When a number moves for
honesty reasons, this site moves with it — the async headline already went from
64.3% to 57.7% that way.
